analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour in two steps.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $6.15 by 2000 was referred to the Senate Labor Committee in March 1998 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $5.15 an hour to $5.65 on January 1, 1999, and then to $6.15 on January 1, 2000 [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Senator Edward Kennedy with 22 Democratic cosponsors and sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee [S1][S4]. The committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage would see their hourly pay rise by $1 over two years, reaching $6.15 in 2000 [S2]. Roughly 7 to 10 million workers earned at or near the minimum wage at the time, so the increase would flow mainly to low-paid workers in retail, restaurants, and other service jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.65 an hour in 1999 and $6.15 an hour in 2000, a $1.00 total increase over the $5.15 rate in effect since 1997 [S2][S3].

The raise applies to all workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act, the same law that sets overtime rules, so it reaches the lowest-paid workers nationwide rather than only in states that set higher state minimums [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay at or near the minimum wage — restaurants, retail stores, farms, and small businesses with low-wage staff — would face higher payroll costs, which they could meet through higher prices, reduced hours, or slower hiring. Studies of past increases generally found modest employment effects, but the cost falls on these businesses and is partly passed to their customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retailers, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Higher mandated wages raise costs for small businesses and restaurants with thin margins, and some economists argue that pushes them to cut hours, automate, or hire fewer entry-level workers.
A one-size-fits-all national wage means the same dollar amount applies in low-cost rural areas and expensive cities, so the bite is much bigger where local wages and prices are lower.
The bill contained no small-business tax offsets or phase-in flexibility; its two-step increase took effect within ten months of introduction, giving employers limited adjustment time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and easy to see: about $2,000 a year more for a full-time minimum-wage worker by 2000. The costs fall on a concentrated set of low-wage employers and partly on consumers through prices, and the evidence from prior federal increases suggests modest job effects rather than large ones. On balance the bill was a straightforward transfer from low-wage employers to low-wage workers; its main design weakness was the lack of any offset for small businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor Committee in March 1998, the committee never scheduled action on it, and it died there when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced the bill on March 19, 1998, with 22 Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1][S3][S5].
The committee took no further action: no markup, no vote, no report back to the Senate [S5].
Kennedy gave introductory remarks again on September 3, 1998, but the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay at or near the minimum wage kept the $5.15 rate in place, and the low-wage workers who would have received the $1 raise never got it. The bill's failure left the floor of the labor market where it was.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks for it in March and again in September 1998.

for.name: 22 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Democratic Leader Tom Daschle.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. James Jeffords (R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in March 1998 and never held a markup or voted to report it out, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats; no Senate Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: Restaurants employ the largest share of minimum-wage workers, so the two-step raise would have raised their payroll costs directly. Industry groups opposed federal increases and backed keeping the rate at $5.15.
Retail is the other big employer of near-minimum-wage labor; the increase would raise costs, partly offset by higher spending from the workers themselves.
The bill offered no tax credits or small-business offsets to cushion the higher wage bill [S3].
